pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Pushes & Pulls

- **Standards — UK (DfE — no discrete KS1 forces unit; first statutory at Year 3):** England has no Key Stage 1 forces programme of study — 'forces as pushes or pulls' is first statutory at Year 3 (KS2). At 5–6 push/pull is met informally through play and EYFS 'Understanding the World', alongside the statutory KS1 Working Scientifically skills (observing closely, performing simple tests).

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-PS2-1; DCI PS2.A):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1] (assessment limited to relative strengths OR directions, not both at once, and excludes non-contact pushes/pulls such as magnets). DCI PS2.A: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1, K-PS2-2].

- **Operational details:** At ages 5-6, forces are introduced concretely as PUSHES and PULLS: actions that can start an object moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or change its direction. Children compare a gentle push with a strong push on the same object (bigger push → bigger change) and notice that an object tends to move in the direction it is pushed or pulled. The teaching is overwhelmingly hands-on — children act on real objects and describe what happens. Crucially, this is where the lifelong 'impetus' misconception is seeded (the idea that a moving thing carries a 'force' inside it that runs out), so even at this age good teaching frames a push/pull as something ONE thing does to ANOTHER, and gently introduces that things stop because something pushes back (friction), not because the push 'runs out'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Lead with hands-on play: push/pull toy cars, balls, trolleys, doors, swings, drawers — children feel and cause the effect before naming it.
Use precise words from the start — push, pull, force — and narrate effects ('your push made it speed up / change direction').
Predict-then-do: 'Which way will it go? What if you push harder?' then act and compare — building evidence for strength and direction effects.
Compare systematically: same object, vary ONE thing (gentle vs strong; push from different sides) so the effect of strength and of direction is isolated.
Start from children's own ideas as 'anchoring conceptions' to build on, rather than just correcting wrong statements (sense-making conversation).
Begin to counter the impetus seed: when something rolls to a stop, attribute it to a push-back from the ground/air (friction), not to force 'running out'.
keyRepresentations: Real manipulable objects (the primary 'representation' at this age — balls, cars, trolleys)
Simple direction arrows showing which way the push/pull acts (seed of the force-arrow representation)
Before/after motion pictures (object at rest → moving; fast → slow)
commonMisconceptions: Only living/animate things can push or pull (a table or wall can't exert a force).
There is only a force if you can see movement — a push that doesn't visibly move something 'isn't a force'.
Impetus seed: a moving object has 'force' or 'go' stored inside it that gradually runs out, which is why it stops (MOSART; RESPeCT Grade 3).
Force is the same as the object's energy / a property the object owns, rather than an interaction between two objects.
A bigger push makes something go faster and faster forever (constant push → ever-increasing or fixed speed confusion, in seed form).

learn.summary: Help 5-6 year-olds experience that a push or pull is a force one thing does to another that can start, stop, speed up, slow down, or turn an object, and that a bigger push makes a bigger change. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes. Centre real hands-on play with objects, predict-then-do comparisons that vary one thing at a time, and begin to attribute stopping to a push-back from the ground/air (friction) rather than a force 'running out'. Screen or picture activities act as complements and light checks, not replacements for physical play.

activities.title: Flick-and-push play: feel a bigger push make a bigger change
feedback: When a child says 'it went faster', reflect the cause: 'Your bigger push made it speed up more.'
If a child thinks every push is the same, line up two identical balls at rest, tap one and shove the other, race them, and let them see strength map to speed before naming it.

If a child says the heavy and light ball move the same with the same push, repeat the same gentle push on two similar-sized balls and watch together. When the lighter ball goes faster or further, name it: 'The same push makes a bigger change to the lighter ball.'
When something rolls to a stop on the floor or carpet, say the ground (or carpet/air) is pushing back and rubbing against it to slow it, rather than the push 'running out'.
(Optional screen cue) A soft coast-to-stop with a 'the ground pushes back' prompt can quietly reinforce that things stop because something opposes them.
activities.rationale: The concept is cause-and-effect on motion, so children should act on real objects and immediately observe the response; varying one thing (gentle vs strong, same push on heavy vs light, or push direction) isolates each effect. An interactive screen version can let a child vary strength and direction and see the object respond, but it complements rather than replaces physical play.
sourceClaims: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Push and pull real objects (balls, toy cars, trolleys, a door, a drawer) and say out loud what happened: did it start, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction?
With two identical balls at rest, tap one gently and shove the other hard at the same time; watch which travels faster and further.

With the same gentle push (for example, the same flick from the same spot), compare a heavier ball and a lighter ball of about the same size (for example, a solid rubber ball and a hollow plastic ball), and notice how far and fast each goes. The same push usually changes the lighter ball's motion more.

Push a ball from different sides and notice that, from rest, it moves off in the direction you pushed it; once it is rolling, give it a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Predict before acting: 'Which way will it go? What happens if I push harder?' Then do it and compare with your prediction.

(Optional screen companion) In a tap-and-flick play space, drag a stretchy aimer back further to push harder and release to send a ball off; set up a side-by-side 'gentle vs strong' race on identical balls and watch the hard-pushed one go faster and further.
activities.intendedInsight: A push or pull is a force that changes how an object moves; a stronger push makes a bigger change to the motion. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes.

activities.title: Compare smooth vs rough: why things stop
feedback: If a child predicts 'the same because I pushed the same', point to the carpet stopping the ball sooner and name the rough surface rubbing as the cause.
If a child explains continued rolling by a push 'stored inside', gently point to the floor/carpet rubbing as what slows it; expect this idea to come back and revisit it on slippery vs rough floors.
When a cushion slows the already-rolling ball, name it: 'The cushion pushed back against the ball and slowed it — that push changed its motion.'
activities.rationale: Comparing the same push on two surfaces sets up friction as an observable cause of stopping (both surfaces here have appreciable friction, which is why the ball slows and stops) and begins to counter the 'impetus' idea that a moving object carries a force that runs out. Formal inertia is not taught at this age.
sourceClaims: Elementary students believe a moving object contains a force given by an outside source and stops when that force 'runs out'; force is wrongly seen as a property inside the object rather than an interaction between two objects.

Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and then on a rough carpet.
Before each roll, predict which will travel further and say why.
Watch the carpet ball stop sooner and talk about what was different between the two surfaces.
Try to slow a ball that is already rolling toward you without catching it (for example, hold a cushion in its path).
activities.intendedInsight: Things slow and stop because a surface (or air) rubs against them and pushes back — friction — not because the push is used up inside the object.

activities.title: Pushes slow and turn, not just start
feedback: If a child says a push can only make things go or go faster, demonstrate a cushion pushing against an already-rolling ball (slowing) and a sideways tap on a rolling ball (bending its path), and name both as the push changing the motion.
Reinforce by asking the child to narrate each effect in their own words.
activities.rationale: Children often think a push can only start or speed up motion; demonstrating slowing and turning as the same force broadens their idea of what a force does. This addresses a documented misconception for this age.
sourceClaims: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Take a ball that is already rolling and find a way to slow it down before it arrives (hold a cushion in its path).
Give a ball that is already rolling a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Say which of these a push can do: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction — and show an example of each with a real object.
activities.intendedInsight: A push or pull is the same kind of force whether it starts, speeds up, slows, stops, or turns an object; slowing and turning are the force acting, not something different.

activities.title: Name pushes and pulls around us
feedback: Confirm correct sorts and, for mistakes, mime the action together to decide whether you are pushing away or pulling toward.
When predicting direction for an object at rest, link it back: 'If the push is strong enough and nothing holds it in place, it starts to move the way the push points.'
activities.rationale: Picture sorts and scene labelling are good vocabulary companions and a light check of direction prediction, but they do not let a child feel that a harder push makes a bigger change, so they supplement physical play rather than carry the core idea. Reading load is a real constraint at 5-6, so use audio or adult support.
learnerActions: Sort picture cards of everyday actions into PUSH and PULL (with an adult reading or audio support).
Look at a playground or home scene and point out where someone is pushing and where someone is pulling (for example, pulling a child on a swing, pushing a trolley).
For a pictured object at rest about to be pushed, point which way it will start to move.
Use the words push, pull, and force as you describe what is happening.
activities.intendedInsight: Pushes and pulls happen all around us; naming them and reading the direction of the force builds the vocabulary that supports the hands-on experiences.

constraints: Keep the teaching overwhelmingly hands-on with real objects; screen and picture activities complement, not replace, physical push/pull play.
Picture sorts and recognition activities can support vocabulary and direction prediction, but do not elicit the child independently producing and feeling a push; pair them with physical play.
Reading load is a real constraint at 5-6; use audio support or an adult reader for any picture-sort activity.
Do not teach formal inertia or Newtonian terminology; frame everything concretely as what one thing does to another.
Frame a push/pull as something ONE thing does to ANOTHER object, and attribute stopping to a push-back (friction), to avoid seeding the 'force runs out' / 'force stored inside' misconception.
The 'impetus' idea is expected to return; plan to revisit and gently re-challenge it across contexts rather than expecting a single correction to settle it.

A push strong enough to move a free object at rest, such as a ball, starts it moving in the push direction (objects on a hinge or track, like a door or drawer, can only move the way they are guided); a sideways tap on an already-rolling ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes (away from the tapping hand) — do not imply a single side push instantly makes travel point exactly in the push direction. State the object's starting motion (at rest or already rolling) whenever predicting an effect.
The smooth/rough coasting comparison models surfaces with appreciable friction, which is why the ball slows and stops; name that rubbing as the cause rather than a used-up push.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled the 3D 'knock-over-the-blocks' option as adding 'production cost without conceptual gain' and the conversation format as unable to deliver the experience; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried in as universal claims. Tactile 3D or spatial play can be worthwhile if that experience is itself a goal.

The claim that 'live recompute is the whole point' and that a static scene 'cannot' teach the strength effect is a catalog preference; retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance (interactive feedback makes the effect vivid), not as proof that static media cannot teach it.
Two of the three sources (MOSART and RESPeCT Grade 3) are marked verified:false in the row; treat the impetus/friction claims as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The 'correctAnswer' in the assessment frames a strong push as what makes a ball reach the target 'quickly'; this is fine as an age-appropriate speed/direction link, but note that at this age children should reason about changes to motion rather than steady-state speed.

The same-push heavy-vs-light comparison is taught in the conventional age-appropriate form (the lighter object moves more for the same push); it is a simple demonstration, not a friction-controlled result.

Summary and the first activity's intendedInsight originally stated unconditionally that the push direction sets the direction of travel; this has been scoped to starting an object from rest (with a sideways tap bending a moving object's path) to match the physics and the stated constraints.

assess.poeTask: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and on a rough carpet. Before rolling, ask the child to predict which travels further and WHY. Many predict 'the same, because I pushed the same' or 'it stops when the push runs out'; seeing the carpet ball stop sooner sets up friction (the ground rubbing) as the cause rather than a used-up push.
probeDeeper: If you push it only gently, will it still reach me? What will be different?
Now it's rolling toward me — show me a way to slow it down before it arrives, without catching it.
A heavy football and a light beach ball each get the same push — will they move the same? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Give it a hard/strong push in my direction. A stronger push makes it speed up more, so a hard push makes it go faster than a gentle one; the push is the force that starts it moving and sets how fast it goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'How hard you push doesn't change anything — a little tap and a big shove make it roll the same.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up two identical balls, tap one gently and shove the other, and race them so the child SEES strength map to speed, then name it.
errorPatterns.distractor: It doesn't matter how hard you push — the ball rolls the same either way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In tier 2 the child cannot say a stronger push gives more speed; treats every push as equivalent.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The ball keeps rolling because the push is still inside it, and it stops when the push runs out.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't teach formal inertia; point to the floor/carpet rubbing (friction) as what slows it, and revisit on a slippery vs rough floor. Expect this idea to return and challenge it repeatedly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains continued motion by a force stored in the ball rather than the hand's push having ended.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A push can only make something go or go faster — it can't slow something down or turn it.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate a cushion pushing against a rolling ball (slowing) and a sideways tap (turning); name both as the push changing the motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to slow or steer a rolling ball, says you can only stop it by grabbing it, or that a push can't change direction.

responseLevels.gap: Says only 'push it' with no link between how hard the push is and how the ball moves, or claims the push amount is irrelevant; may say a push can't slow or turn things.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a push or pull is a force that changes motion and that a bigger force makes a bigger change — a strong push speeds it up more, an opposing push slows it, a sideways push turns it — and predicts direction from the direction of the push, transferring to a new object.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a harder push makes it go faster and can aim the push toward the target, but treats a push only as 'making it go' — lists effects (start, faster) without seeing slowing and turning as the same force acting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: This ball is sitting still on the floor. If you want it to roll over to me quickly, what would you do to it — and why does doing that make it go fast instead of slow?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tell is in the 'why'. A child who grasps that a force changes motion connects a HARDER push to MORE speed and aims the push toward the target. A child who thinks the amount of push doesn't matter, that you must push repeatedly, or that only certain 'strong' things can make it move gives the same first answer ('push it') but a reason that shows no force-to-effect link. Both children say 'push it'; only the reason separates them.

sources.claim: Students think a force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed (a constant force gives constant speed); the correction is that at constant speed the forces add to zero. These intuitive ideas must be challenged repeatedly across many contexts.
sources.source: IOP Spark (Institute of Physics) — 'Many students think that a force is needed to keep an object moving with a constant speed'

sources.claim: Elementary students believe a moving object contains a force given by an outside source and stops when that force 'runs out'; force is wrongly seen as a property inside the object rather than an interaction between two objects.
sources.source: Harvard-Smithsonian MOSART — elementary physical-science misconceptions; BSCS/RESPeCT Grade 3 Forces module

sources.claim: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
